motion: What is the best account of objective morality?

bridges.description: Show that God is the best ultimate ground of objective morality.
Explain moral value through God's Trinitarian loving nature.
Explain obligation and moral knowledge through personal divine relations and creation.
Show that objective morality can be fundamental without a divine foundation.
Explain goodness and obligation through intrinsic moral features and reasons.
Explain how evolved thinkers can gain reliable access to necessary moral truths.

sections.title: Ultimate foundations and stopping points
sections.rationale: The central motion-level dispute is whether God or fundamental moral truths provide the better terminus of explanation.

sections.title: Non-natural properties and intrinsic value
sections.rationale: The exchange tests whether moral value belongs intrinsically to concrete relations or requires divine grounding.

sections.title: Goodness, obligation, and accountability
sections.rationale: The speakers distinguish value from duty and test whether personal divine authority is needed for obligation.

sections.title: Evolution and access to moral truth
sections.rationale: The final exchange addresses whether unguided evolution can yield reliable moral beliefs.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: A theistic account also appears to rely on an unexplained moral axiom: that Trinitarian love is good.
moves.warrant: If that goodness has no further explanation, theism and non-theistic realism both ultimately appeal to foundational moral truths.
moves.inference: The alleged explanatory advantage of grounding everything in God is reduced.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins when Wielenberg states that every objective-morality theory likely contains moral axioms and ends with his complete question about what makes Trinitarian love good; the retained setup is necessary to show why the question challenges theism's claimed explanatory advantage.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator gives Wielenberg the first direct question, he addresses Adam by name, and the uninterrupted question continues through E0977.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This attacks the claimed difference between divine grounding and Wielenberg's fundamental moral axioms.

burdenContact.rationale: If theism also terminates in a moral axiom, a non-theistic stopping point loses a central comparative disadvantage.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: God himself, rather than an ungrounded moral proposition, is the ultimate stopping point.
moves.warrant: Facts about God's triune loving character describe the ultimate being; humans call that character good and discover it as the ultimate good.
moves.inference: The account grounds moral truth in a concrete supreme being rather than free-standing axioms.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers Johnson's complete answer from his explicit disagreement through the distinction between God and facts about God, then his direct account of why Trinitarian love is called good. The length is required because both the ontological stopping point and the goodness challenge must be answered together.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the ultimate good is what God is like.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson begins immediately after Wielenberg's question at E0978 and speaks without a substantive handoff until the moderator takes the next turn.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies Johnson's central positive account of the ultimate ground and answers the strongest first challenge to it.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies God himself as the ultimate reality in which moral truth is grounded.

responseComponents.description: Denies that the goodness claim is an ungrounded moral axiom and locates ultimacy in God himself.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Wielenberg's non-natural account needs to explain what non-natural means and why atheists should accept it.
moves.warrant: Its departure from physicalism makes it controversial among atheists.
moves.inference: The account bears an explanatory burden concerning the status of moral properties.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's full two-part question: what non-natural means and whether that feature alienates physicalist atheists.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the next question to Adam; Johnson names Eric and asks an uninterrupted question through E1072.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This tests the ontological intelligibility and constituency-facing cost of Wielenberg's account.

burdenContact.rationale: It presses whether the rival account can explain the kind of reality its moral properties occupy.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Objective moral features are real but are not physical features discoverable by empirical science.
moves.warrant: Wrongness appears categorically different from mass or volume; moral reality seems real while resisting physical reduction.
moves.inference: A non-natural moral category is more plausible than either denying morality or reducing it to physics.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's explicit rejection of materialism and scientism, preserves his distinction between science and scientism, explains why moral features are not physical, and includes his answer that physicalist atheists reject the view. The extended span is needed to retain both requested parts and the inference from apparently real but nonphysical morality.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson's question ends at E1072; Wielenberg begins the answer at E1073 and remains the uninterrupted speaker until the moderator's next handoff.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Wielenberg's direct account of the metaphysical status of objective moral properties.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains how objective moral reality can be fundamental without being physical or divine.

responseComponents.description: Defines non-natural moral features and accepts, while answering, the objection from physicalist atheists.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: A mother's love for her baby appears intrinsically good and asks whether Johnson must deny its value without God.
moves.warrant: Its goodness seems contained in the loving relationship rather than derived from an external source.
moves.inference: Intrinsic value presents a direct rival to divine grounding.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Preserves Wielenberg's definition of intrinsic value, his mother-and-baby example, and the complete question whether such love would lack value without a triune God; stops before the mixed handoff E1236.
moves.attributionRationale: After the moderator assigns Wielenberg the next question, he speaks continuously through E1235; mixed E1236 is excluded.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This presents intrinsic value as a concrete competitor to value derived from God.

burdenContact.rationale: The example tests whether value can reside in a loving relation itself.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Without God, motherly love would more plausibly be a survival-producing subjective adaptation than an intrinsic non-natural value.
moves.warrant: On Johnson's view God grounds all reality; under the contrary hypothetical, evolutionary selection explains caregiving feelings without supplying objective value.
moves.inference: The hypothetical does not establish intrinsic goodness independently of God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins when Johnson grants the hypothetical for argument's sake and runs it through his evolutionary alternative; earlier remarks only explain his difficulty imagining a Godless reality. The selected span preserves his qualifications that the hypothetical is implausible and, in his view, impossible.
moves.attributionRationale: After the excluded mixed handoff E1236, frozen ownership assigns Johnson's uninterrupted answer E1237–E1321.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Johnson's substantive answer to the proposed intrinsic-value counterexample.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that a Godless account better explains love feelings adaptively than as objective intrinsic value.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the hypothetical only for argument and offers evolutionary adaptation as the rival explanation of motherly love.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Wielenberg owes reasons and evidence for treating brute non-natural moral axioms as an ultimate stopping point.
moves.warrant: God has teleological and cosmological arguments offered on his behalf, while brute axioms seem merely asserted.
moves.inference: Competing stopping points should be compared by explanatory support.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's comparison of ultimate stopping points and the full request for reasons and evidence for non-natural moral axioms.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator gives Adam the next question; Johnson speaks continuously from E1324 through E1376.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This asks for positive comparative support for Wielenberg's proposed foundation.

burdenContact.rationale: It contrasts arguments offered for God with the asserted fundamentality of moral axioms.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Given Wielenberg's disputed premise that theistic accounts also contain moral axioms, accepting objective morality commits either account to some fundamental moral axioms.
moves.warrant: Objective morality appears real, inference to the best explanation favors basic axioms, and Wielenberg argues that every objective-morality theory—including Johnson's, if his earlier critique is right—contains them.
moves.inference: Conditionally, if Johnson's theory cannot avoid moral axioms, the choice is not God versus brute axioms but objective morality with axioms versus abandoning objective morality.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Preserves both parts of Wielenberg's answer: inference to the best explanation and his explicit E1429–E1436 qualification that the argument depends on the unresolved dispute over whether Johnson's account contains axioms.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson's question ends at E1376; Wielenberg answers uninterrupted from E1377 through E1436.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies Wielenberg's positive and explicitly conditional defense of foundational axioms.

burdenContact.rationale: It defends axioms as an unavoidable stopping point only if the same commitment is present in the rival theistic theory.

responseComponents.description: Offers abductive support for axioms while making the equal-footing argument conditional on the disputed theistic-axiom premise.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Explaining why obedience resembles divine goodness does not yet explain its mustness or obligatory force.
moves.warrant: Obligation has a mustness or requirement that goodness by itself does not appear to contain.
moves.inference: Johnson must identify what converts good obedience into a requirement.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Wielenberg's reconstruction of Johnson's view and his complete distinction between goodness and obligatory mustness, ending with the direct question about what creates the requirement.
moves.attributionRationale: Wielenberg is assigned the next question and addresses Adam continuously from E1440 through E1467.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This isolates whether Johnson explains obligation rather than only moral value.

burdenContact.rationale: The move tests whether value resemblance can generate the distinct normative force of duty.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Johnson accepts that goodness and obligation are distinct, illustrates the difference with a good but non-obligatory orphanage project, and argues that loving obedience grounds obligation in divine value.
moves.warrant: Moral theories must explain both value and duty; God is the exemplar of goodness, Trinitarian love supplies the value standard, and obedience is intertwined with loving God.
moves.inference: Johnson's account aims to connect obligation to value through loving resemblance, though his stated endpoint specifically explains why obedience is good.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Johnson's explicit statement of the dispute, retains his acceptance and orphanage illustration of the goodness/obligation distinction, and continues through his answer that loving obedience resembles Trinitarian love. The length is required to preserve both the conceded distinction and his proposed bridge.
moves.attributionRationale: Wielenberg's question ends at E1467; Johnson takes the answer at E1468 and continues until the moderator's next handoff.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Johnson's direct attempt to bridge the value-duty distinction pressed by Wielenberg.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects human duty to the personal relation of loving and obeying God.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the distinction, illustrates it with a beyond-duty good act, and proposes loving obedience as the connection between value and obligation.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Abstract moral objects are poor stopping points because they cry out for an explanation.
moves.warrant: Traditions that posit abstract truths have often sought a theistic source, and arguments infer God from such objects.
moves.inference: God offers a deeper explanation than unexplained Platonic entities.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's question whether Wielenberg still needs Platonic abstract objects and his argument that such objects themselves call for explanation; ends before mixed E1607.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator gives Adam the next question; Johnson speaks continuously through E1606, with mixed E1607 excluded.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This presses whether the rival stopping point is metaphysically self-explanatory.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that apparently abstract moral truths point beyond themselves toward a divine source.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: The account needs concrete things with objective moral features but need not require separate abstract objects.
moves.warrant: A mother's love can be intrinsically good whether or not a disputed ontology of abstract properties is correct.
moves.inference: Rejecting Platonic entities does not remove fundamental rightness, wrongness, goodness, and badness.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's statement of the abstract-object dispute, preserves the concrete-property distinction and his willingness to abandon Platonism, and ends with the claim that particular things retain unsourced moral features. The extended explanation is necessary because the answer separates optional abstract entities from the essential moral properties.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a mother's love for her child is intrinsically good.
moves.attributionRationale: After mixed E1607 is excluded, Wielenberg's answer begins at E1608 and continues uninterrupted through E1712.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This removes abstract-object ontology from the essential commitments of Wielenberg's moral realism.

burdenContact.rationale: It locates value in concrete things and relations regardless of the separate Platonism debate.

responseComponents.description: Concedes that Platonism is optional and denies that the moral account depends on unexplained abstract objects.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Johnson should clarify whether obligation exists only when wrongdoing brings punishment or accountability.
moves.warrant: His published formulation links guilt and accountability to a personal moral authority.
moves.inference: The grounding of duty must be distinguished from consequences for breach.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Wielenberg's quoted accountability premise and his precise clarification question distinguishing moral obligation from punishment or getting in trouble.
moves.attributionRationale: Wielenberg announces the shift in topic and asks Johnson an uninterrupted question from E1716 through E1738.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This tests whether Johnson makes accountability constitutive of obligation.

burdenContact.rationale: It separates the existence of a duty from enforcement consequences.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Obligations arise because God created humans to love God and others; divine judgment adds accountability but is not presented as the sole generator of duty.
moves.warrant: Loving and obeying God are intertwined, while God also appropriately judges and punishes evil.
moves.inference: Personal purpose grounds obligation and divine authority accounts for accountability.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers Johnson's answer that created purpose and loving relations generate obligation, then his distinct claim that God as judge adds accountability and punishment. It stops after completing the accountability point, omitting the subsequent salvation detail as unnecessary to the answer.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson begins immediately after Wielenberg's clarification question and speaks continuously through the selected completion of his judgment account.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This states Johnson's personal grounding of duty and distinguishes it from God's enforcement role.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds obligation in God's purpose for persons and accountability in God's authority as judge.

responseComponents.description: Denies that punishment alone generates obligation, locating duty in created loving purpose while retaining divine accountability.

moves.speaker: Adam Lloyd Johnson
moves.claim: Unguided evolution makes the match between human moral beliefs and independent non-natural truths appear coincidental.
moves.warrant: Different evolutionary paths could have produced very different beliefs, while theism can explain alignment through God.
moves.inference: Wielenberg needs a non-theistic account of reliable moral knowledge.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Johnson's complete lucky-coincidence objection: independent moral truths, unguided evolutionary belief formation, possible alternative paths, and the resulting reliability challenge.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator identifies Adam's final question; Johnson presents it uninterrupted from E1829 through E1898.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the principal epistemic challenge to Wielenberg's non-theistic realism.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that theism explains moral-belief reliability while unguided evolution appears not to.

moves.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
moves.claim: Moral-belief alignment is imperfect, but necessary moral truths plus partly directional evolutionary pressures and ordinary generalization can explain the degree of alignment that exists.
moves.warrant: The axioms could not have differed; human beliefs vary through evolution, culture, and experience; survival favors recognizing one's own pain and rights, while a useful similarity-based inference extends comparable status to others.
moves.inference: With these qualifications, unguided evolution can move thinkers toward some moral truths without the degree of luck alleged by the objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins with Wielenberg's short answer, preserves his concession that beliefs do not align perfectly, his nature-and-nurture qualifications, and the complete two-stage mechanism through E2007. The long span is necessary because omitting any of those qualifications would overstate the proposed evolutionary reliability account.
moves.attributionRationale: Johnson's final question ends at E1898; Wielenberg answers continuously from E1899 through the last substantive event E2007.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is required for this high-confidence turn attribution.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Wielenberg's complete answer to the central epistemic objection against his account.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains limited moral knowledge through fixed truths, selected self-regarding beliefs, and generalization rather than divine guidance.

responseComponents.description: Concedes imperfect correspondence and offers a qualified evolutionary and inferential mechanism for the alignment that remains.
